Mr. Chairman, I should
like to continue the remarks I was making when the committee adjourned for the dinner
Supply-Labour
recess at six o'clock. I had made some reference to compulsory conciliation and compulsory arbitration. I pointed out that compulsory conciliation is a fundamental part of Canada's labour legislation. There is, I think, a feeling in some quarters that the purpose of the provisions of our compulsory conciliation legislation is to allow what is called a cooling-off period so that "rash" trade unionists or perhaps "irresponsible" trade unionists will not do something irresponsible or something rash.
Personally, I prefer to think that there is a better principle than that behind the legislation. I believe that the legislation rests on the principle that industrial disputes are not merely matters that concern labour and employers. I am convinced that industrial disputes concern more than labour and employers and that contention is well demonstrated in the industrial dispute that brought us here last fall.
Industrial disputes today concern the community; and I believe that the compulsory conciliation legislation rests on the principle that the community is involved in any strike or lock-out because such actions affect the community. The government, as spokesman for the people of Canada, says that employers and organized labour cannot be allowed to deal with matters of this kind as if they were the only people concerned; it says that there is a community interest and that it is going to see to it that, as far as possible, the community interest is protected. There are, therefore, various stages which a dispute must go through before a strike or lock-out takes place. When these are finally complied with, and if a settlement has not been arrived at, a strike may take place. These procedures perhaps serve the purpose of providing a cooling-off period; but they also serve the purpose of getting employers and employees together, in a good atmosphere, to talk over their differences. That is a good thing. Not many disputes end in strike action after they have gone through our procedure of conciliation.
There is something else I should like to say. It will be forty-one years this summer -within a month or so-since I first became connected with the trade union movement; and I have been fairly closely associated with it ever since, even although for the last twenty years I have not been engaged in an occupation in which I had to carry a union card. People whose experience with labour matters dates back to, say 1929 or a little earlier-and I imagine there are quite a number of them in this committee-have no realization of the improvements that have taken place in the status of trade

Supply-Labour
unions in Canada during the last forty years, and more particularly during the last ten years. As I mentioned before, the reason that the progress was made during the last ten years is that organized labour was in a position in which it seldom finds itself except in wartime, namely, that of full employment. Consequently, when its services are urgently required by the country, it can improve its position by withholding its labour, which up until now at least, had been its ultimate weapon of defence and offence.
I have seen an employer refusing to deal with a trade union because the trade union had international connections; that is, it was connected with a trade union in the United States. And I have seen the same employer refusing to deal with the trade union because it did not have international connections. Any pretext at all was used to avoid recognizing the trade union movement and entering into collective agreements. When I first became connected with the trade union movement employers, by and large, took the position that they were going to run their businesses in their own way and that they were not going to be interfered with by a bunch of irresponsible trade unionists.
As far as I know, there is only one way of developing responsibility and that is by giving responsibility. If a person has nothing to be responsible about, he can be irresponsible. But the moment that he is put in the position in which certain events hang on his actions, he will be much more careful how he acts. Over the last fifty years we have built up in Canada a trade union movement which is today a great asset to the country. In it are men of experience, understanding and responsibility. I should like to see this government take more advantage of their experience than it has taken heretofore. Every year the organized labour movement through its various sections, makes submissions to the government as to the legislation that it would like to see enacted. It should be noted that nearly all of this legislation refers not to the trade union movement itself but to the community at large. That is, of course, all to the good because it means that the organized labour movement is extending its horizons from its own immediate affairs and is realizing that it cannot prosper unless the whole community prospers.
I mentioned the fact that the national bodies of organized labour each year make submissions to the government. I should like to look forward to the day when the government would not only receive organized labour when it comes to make its submission, but would send for organized labour and

ask it to give its views on the important questions of the day. When that day comes, I believe that our democracy will have advanced far beyond what it is today. However, under the conditions that we have today where labour is considered a commodity-if it is not considered that in theory; it is considered so in fact-and where a person has access to the means of life only so long as he can sell his labour, a position in which most of us find ourselves, when he is unemployed, even with unemployment insurance, for any lengthy period of time, his position and the position of his family are difficult indeed.
I think we have come to the time-perhaps we have not heard much about it yet, but there has been some talk about it- when instead of the daily wage, the hourly wage, the weekly wage or the monthly wage, workers will have an annual wage, so that they will know from one year to the next where they stand. Why should a railroad man, a street railway employee or a longshoreman or a lumber worker not have an annual wage as well as a bank manager, a railroad executive, a bank employee, a school teacher, a university professor or any of the numerous people who have annual wages or an annual salary. I think that we have to prepare ourselves for greater advances in that regard than we have seen heretofore.
The matter of unemployment insurance was raised today, and I want to say just a few words about it. One of the things that the government should do in regard to uniemployment insurance is to tell the people more about it. They should do a better job of public relations in the matter of unemployment insurance than they are doing. As a matter of fact, in this house where one would expect a higher level of intelligence or understanding on questions of this kind than you may find generally among the community, since it is one of our jobs to deal with the matter, not enough is known about our unemployment insurance. It was mentioned that a person pays into the unemployment insurance fund and never takes anything out of it. Well, if everyone who paid into the unemployment insurance fund took something out, or took out what he paid in, the unemployment insurance contributions would have to be very much larger than they are today.
The principle of insurance is that you take something out provided that what you are insured against happens; and if that does not happen you consider yourself lucky. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre says if you take out fire insurance on your

house, generally you consider yourself fortunate if you never draw any insurance- that is never have a fire. The same thing is true of automobile accident insurance. You consider yourself fortunate if you never have to call on the insurance company for payments in connection with an accident. Unemployment insurance is insurance for involuntary unemployment. In that regard I believe that the procedure could be considerably improved. May I point out something that may not be known by hon. members, and perhaps some will not believe it, particularly on the government side of the house. Like almost everything else that we get from this government, we got unemployment insurance not because they believed in it as a good thing socially; we got it in 1940 because prices were going up. It was instituted more to stemv inflation than as a piece of desirable social legislation. The reason I say that is this. The trade union movement had been advocating unemployment insurance for thirty years before it was put on the statute books. Mind you, there were many, many occasions when unemployment insurance could have been very useful. In the 1930's governments said they could not bring unemployment insurance in because they did not have the money. That applied to the Conservatives as well as to the Liberals. They were like the man who when he was asked why he did not shingle his house said that he did not shingle it because it rained. He was then asked why he did not shingle it when it was not raining, and he said when it did not rain it did not leak. That was the attitude and I am very much afraid it is still the attitude.
I believe that unemployment insurance should be extended to every worker, at least to every worker who is working for an employer. It was said today, and it was said in the house the other evening in another debate, that the labour force in Canada is
5.200.000.	May I say that 5,200,000 includes not only what we refer to generally as workers, but it includes employers as well. I hold in my hand the unemployment insurance report for the year ended March 31, 1950. I believe it is the last one that has been distributed, and it gives the labour force as
5.200.000.	But, as I said, that includes employers to the number of 226,000; unpaid family workers to the number of 306,000. Also included in that figure are own-account workers to the number of 941,000. That makes a total of 1,473,000. It would be rather difficult to include that million and a half approximately in an unemployment insurance scheme such as ours. But there are wage earners to the number of 1,097,000 who
80709-173J
Supply-Labour
are not insured. I believe that those wage earners should be insured, and that insurance should be paid to everyone who is out of work for reasons beyond his own control and who has fulfilled certain conditions.
I am not going to express an opinion as to whether present conditions are satisfactory or not, but as long as our unemployment insurance is on an actuarial basis we shall have to give consideration to the number of contributions and so on. I do not know that there is anything further I have to say. There are a dozen questions that could be discussed and that, perhaps, if they are raised, I shall have something to say about. But I shall conclude at this time by impressing upon the minister that his department or the unemployment insurance commission should make a better job of public relations with the unemployment insurers, so that those who are insured may know exactly what they are entitled to, and what they are not entitled to. I find there is a great deal of misunderstanding on that point.
It would be well to visit trade union meetings, or to have representatives of the commission go to those meetings, and to have posters in trade union halls and in the offices of trade union organizations; because the more people understand about their affairs- and unemployment insurance is their affair- the better for all, and the more easily those affairs can be administered.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to debate this matter generally, but rather to draw the minister's attention to a few specific items. First and foremost I would speak about unemployment insurance for fishermen. Various classes and categories of workers have been discussed this afternoon and this evening, and I would now direct the minister's attention to the case for the fishermen.
The matter has already been discussed briefly this session by the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine, and I should like to read what he said on that occasion, as it appears in the last page of the translation appended to Hansard for April 24:
Thirdly, fishermen request unemployment insurance benefits. As early as last spring, one year ago, I made representations to the unemployment insurance commission and the Department of Labour in order to bring fishermen under the act. The unemployment insurance commission began a nation-wide survey to secure the necessary information and data before reporting on this request. I understand that the report is in preparation and hope that the government will be able to include fishermen in the benefits of this legislation which has already been extended to lumberjacks.
I wonder if the minister, when he gets around to it-perhaps not right away-would tell us what has happened to what the hon.

Supply-Labour
member said on that occasion. He will appreciate the difficulty when he understands that while workers in filleting plants come under the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act, the actual producers, the fishermen who bring in the fish so that these people can work, do not. I feel that it is a great injustice. I realize there are difficulties in the way, but I urge a real effort should be made whereby fishermen may be brought within the purview of the act. The minister will, I trust, make some comments in this connection.
I asked the minister a question yesterday to which he was good enough to give an answer. However, so that he will have the background of the difficulty at Seven Islands, I would point out that the original agreement with these companies was passed in 1938 by the then government of Newfoundland, and is set out at page 305 of the Newfoundland Statutes of 1938, No. 41. This was an act taking the place of an agreement between Weaver Minerals Limited and the government of Newfoundland, and substituting the Labrador Mining and Exploration Company Limited for the Weaver Company. Section 45 of the act says:
Except where It is necessary for the company to employ technical experts the company shall at all times employ Newfoundland workmen provided same shall be available.
I believe the minister saw the news item in the Daily News of Newfoundland of April 27, to which I referred yesterday, and which stated:
The majority of the Newfoundlanders who went to Seven Islands several weeks ago to work on the construction of the railway line from Seven Islands to the iron ore deposits have since returned home.
Their story is one of poor living and working conditions. The company, they state, failed to live up to its agreement. There was also friction between the Newfoundlanders and French Canadian workers. The latter outnumbered the Newfoundland workers many times over.
Mr. Harold Horwood, member of the house of assembly for Labrador who until recently was hiring agent for the syndicate engaged in the construction work, stated yesterday that the companies had "failed entirely to live up to their agreement with Newfoundland."
Under the agreement it was agreed by both parties that 1,000 men would be hired from Quebec and an equal number from Newfoundland. These men would work side by side in Quebec territory and in Labrador. This it was hoped would speed the project and eliminate the hiring of Quebec men to work only in Quebec and Newfoundlanders to work only in Labrador.
Many of the men who went to Seven Islands as machine operators were requested to take over other work at a lower rate of pay. They had been promised, at hiring, a specific wage rate. "It seemed," said one of the men, "that the French-Canadian foreman wanted to get rid of the Newfoundlanders and made conditions as tough as possible for us."
Another told of being billeted in a camp where living conditions were anything but the best, with

all French Canadians. The language and customs barrier made it impossible for him to become acquainted with his fellow workers.
Mr. Horwood feels that such conditions will continue to exist until some arrangements can be made between the Newfoundland government and the operating companies whereby a representative for the Newfoundland workers will be on the spot to look after their interest.
The syndicate is comprised of four companies, Cartier, McNamara, Mannix and Morrison-Knudsen.
In his reply yesterday the minister said there is no branch of the national employment service set up there yet, and no accommodation whereby it can be set up. I do not expect the minister to name any date, but I urge upon him that something be done at the earliest possible moment, because the iron ore deposit is one of the great things Newfoundland is counting upon to provide work. It is true that only the skimmed milk will be left for the province; in other words it will benefit materially only from the ordinary work given to the workers. The amounts from royalties are small, and it seems that processing is to be done outside the province.
In view of the fact that we do not worry him very often about these matters I would ask that he endeavour at the earliest possible moment to see that at least our skimmed milk is made available to us as quickly as possible.
The other matter to which I should like to refer has already been mentioned this afternoon. I have in mind the question of the national advisory council on manpower. Let me say at once how pleased we are that the minister saw fit to have a Newfoundlander appointed to that council. We consider it a great compliment, and are satisfied that he will do honour to the council as well. I must confess however that I wish to join with the hon. member for Nanaimo in saying that we are all somewhat worried because they have not got down to work more quickly. I have no doubt the minister is also worried.
Only today I noticed an article in the Montreal Gazette, headed "Labour Pinch Seen in Machine Tools". This is a Canadian Press dispatch dated at Toronto May 3, and stating that Walter G. Hubbard, vice president of a machine tool manufacturing firm, said that he is extremely worried about the situation with respect to machine tool manufacturers. The article goes on to say:
As rearmament accelerated, more and more lathes and precision planes, grinders and drills would be needed. But there were not more and more trained men to make them.
Thus we will be obliged to cut off deliveries to our normal customers (the manufacturers of non-essential goods) and devote all our time to defence.
As the minister well realizes, that is a serious matter. I presume he will get this committee together as quickly as possible. A

rumour seems to be fairly prevalent around this city in the past few days that this committee is to get its information from the census returns. I hope that that is not so. If the people of Canada believe that the information they give in the census is going to be used in that way they may not give the census takers the information they want.

May I say to the hon. member for St. John's East that there is no relation between the advisory committee on manpower and the organization set up to take the census. I make that categorical statement. As I stated on the day I announced the setting up of this advisory committee, we already have throughout the country local advisory committees from which the national body in between its sittings can always get information and pass it on to us.
This recalls something the hon. member for Vancouver East said. First of all I want to express my pleasure at having him give us his philosophy on labour relations as I think that is a most valuable thing to have on the record. The hon. member said that he would like to live to see the day when either the department or the government-I have forgotten which but it does not matter- would consult with leaders of labour as they do with other leaders in connection with matters affecting the welfare of the country. That recalls what the hon. member for Nanaimo and the hon. member for Cape Breton South said this afternoon, that this manpower committee was not meeting often enough. I agree that it may want to meet and may need to meet more often in the future than it has in the past.
However, I would point out that the most effective work is not always done when the members of a committee are sitting around a table. The hon. member for Bow River and the hon. member for Cape Breton South pointed out just what is happening in Windsor, particularly in the automobile industry. The representative of the parent organization of the automobile workers on the national committee is Mr. Pat Conroy. That situation in Windsor had been brought to our attention and as a result some three weeks ago the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who represents that area, and I invited Mr. Burt and some eleven of his chief lieutenants to meet with the Minister of Defence Production, the Minister of Resources and Development, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the hon. member for Essex West, myself and a number of officials to discuss this very question.
I admit that no suggestion was made at that meeting that the government would lift the employees who were presently out of
Supply-Labour
work to some other place, out the Minister of Defence Production outlined at great length and with great care what the plans were to see that the time lost in changing over from cars, say to aeroplane parts, would be no more serious in the way of lost time than the change-over from one model of car to another. As hon. members know, in their wage negotiations the automobile industry take into consideration the fact that there is often a period when groups of men are out of work because of change-overs.
I think I can report with some confidence that the situation is improving, but I did want to make the point that it was not just in the conference room that the advice of the national advisory council on manpower was received.
While the hon. member for St. John's East was speaking a moment ago I consulted with the Minister of Public Works and he has agreed with me to leave nothing undone to have an office of the national employment service established on the island as early as possible.

Mr. Chairman, the number of hon. members who have already referred to the national advisory council on manpower indicates the interest there is at the present time in that body. A year ago, and two years ago, when the minister's estimates were before us we were concerned with the question of unemployment. As has been indicated already, Korea has changed all that and today the country is more concerned with the question of the availability and allocation of manpower that it is with unemployment.
I want to compliment the information branch of the minister's department upon the excellent report they issued on the first meeting of the national advisory council back in February. According to that report the council made excellent progress, on paper at least. I should like to suggest to the minister that he bring us up to date on the work of the council, either tonight or when he has the information available.
According to the report there were six recommendations adopted at the meeting of the council, but the implementation of those recommendations was left on the doorstep of the Department of Labour. Therefore, I presume it will not be difficult for the minister to bring us up to date regarding these recommendations. I am going to enumerate them, not for the minister's benefit but because I think they are excellent recommendations and I am sure the committee will be interested in knowing what has happened in the two and a half months since the council met.

Supply-Labour
The first recommendation was that the records of technical and scientific personnel, which were first assembled in world war II, should be brought up to date, and added to those records there should be a record of all apprentices in Canada, this information to be brought together and studied for the purpose of increasing apprenticeship enrolment. I wonder if the minister can tell us what progress has been made in gathering that record, and what increase or improvement, if any, has taken place in the matter of apprenticeship enrolment.
The next important resolution was that the Department of Labour, in conjunction with other departments, should provide for priority in the placement of persons who apply for employment at the national employment offices. A priority rating was to be prepared, and those applying at the national employment offices were to be directed to the industries standing highest in that priority. I have not heard anything since with respect to what progress has been made in assembling that priority rating. Possibly the minister can tell us what particular industries now have received or are about to receive a high rating in this respect.
A third recommendation which is a matter of great concern to the people of Canada at the present time pertains to the question of national registration. It was agreed that a comprehensive study should be made of all aspects of this questiqp. I think we are very much concerned with this matter, and possibly the minister will inform us whether sufficient information has been secured to enable the government to decide whether or not we are to have a national registration.
One of the recommendations in which I was particularly interested was that some study should be made of the possibility of training the physically handicapped of Canada and thereby enabling them to undertake work of a self-supporting nature. This was to be undertaken as a result of the very excellent conference that was held a few weeks prior to that in Toronto between the federal and provincial authorities where the question of training physically handicapped people was discussed. I think we should know whether there has been any real progress in that respect in the last two and a half months, or whether we are still at the recommendation stage.
The last of the recommendations that I am going to call to the minister's attention was that some study should be given to the possibility first of moving workers from places where they were out of employment to places
fMr. Noseworthy.]
where there was employment. It was suggested that something by way of financial assistance would be given, possibly transportation expenses or something of that kind, to enable workers to move to places where jobs were available. There was also the suggestion that there was to be an examination of the possibility of placing industry near sources of available labour. That is rather a new departure. I think it is the first time that we have heard of consideration being given to moving industry to places where labour is available instead of moving labour to places where work is available. Possibly the minister can tell us what study has been made of the subject and whether anything concrete has yet been achieved in that respect.
There is one other matter on which I would ask the minister to give us a statement if he can. It is a question that is a source of worry to some of the trade unions at the present time. I wrote to the minister about it a few days ago, and I am sure he has not had time yet to reply. I refer to the status of the unions in plants which are working on contracts for defence production and where it becomes necessary to introduce certain security measures, where a security officer is appointed. Sometimes men have to be moved from certain secret types of work because of suspicion and so forth. The questions that the trade unions in my riding have asked me are these:	First
of all is the security officer in such plants appointed by and responsible to any department of the government, or is he appointed by the management of the plant and responsible to them? Do his instructions regarding security measures that are to be taken come from some government department, or do they come from the management of the plant concerned? Out of that arises the status of some groups that are now members of the union, the bargaining party, and in particular the fire protection staffs in these plants. The information which has been given to some of these unions is that fire protection staffs must withdraw from the union. In some of these plants the members of these staffs are members of the union. The understanding has been given to them that they will be required to withdraw from the union because of the nature of the work being done in the plant. Whether these instructions are coming from the government or whether they are devised by some local security officer on his own responsibility, or on the management's responsibility, seems to be uncertain. I would be very pleased if some time during

his estimates the minister would give consideration to these points and pass on that information.
In reply to my hon. friend, under terminable services on page 29 I shall be very glad to give a report on the matter affecting the first report of the national advisory council on manpower.
There is no information available since the report of their first meeting?

My hon. friend asked for a report on the six items which he mentioned tonight. I shall be glad to give that under "terminable services" because it is under that heading that an amount covering their travelling expenses is listed.

I wanted to ask the minister one or two questions about the national advisory council, and I hope he can deal with these questions tonight because the item to which he has just referred may not be up for consideration for many weeks. I think it is customary for the minister to answer questions when they are asked on the administration item, especially when time is of considerable importance.
There has been some discussion today about this advisory council not having been called together for a second time. I would point out to the minister that on February 5 he had this to say with regard to the council, and I am quoting from page 71 of Hansard. for that date:
In this search for the maximum utilization of manpower now under the voluntary system, I believe the government should have available a joint clearing house for the prompt study of month to month manpower resources and needs, for the formulation of advice to the Minister of Labour or to the government with respect to these matters, and for the interpretation of resultant plans to workers, to management and indeed to all citizens.
If the minister will recall, at the time that statement was made the whole question of manpower was of the utmost importance. Nothing has happened, either at home or abroad, in the intervening days to diminish that importance. I am quite sure the minister will agree with that statement. On February 5, which will be three months ago tomorrow, he said he was going to have the advantage of consultation with this advisory council from month to month. I think there has been a great mistake in not having these consultations carried out. I would hope that from now on there would be n.o further such delays.
On February 21, a news release was issued by the minister's department on the subject of the first meeting of the national advisory council on manpower. In that release we find that certain subjects were specifically dealt
Supply-Labour
with, obviously the subjects which were considered the most important by the advisory council when it did have this first meeting. I believe one subject concerned a national registration. In this press release we find the following. It recommends-
-that the departments concerned should make an immediate and comprehensive study of all aspects of the national registration question.
That was the recommendation of this national advisory council on manpower when it met on February 20 and 21 of this year. On that same date press dispatches indicated that work would be started at once on the drafting of a national registration form. I am quoting from the Montreal Gazette of February 21, and the press dispatch states that the draft was to be submitted to the national advisory council on manpower at its next meeting. Unfortunately, of course, there has been no "next meeting". The report goes on:
The meeting will be held in camera, unlike the inaugural session yesterday which was open to the press. It is understood that steps will be taken to place orders for the paper and other materials necessary to turn out large numbers of the national registration forms, if the draft proves unsatisfactory. Present indications are that national registration plans adopted for use in the present emergency will differ materially from those in use during the second world war.
A great deal of emphasis was placed on the fact that this council recommended an immediate comprehensive study of all the aspects of the national registration question. I would ask the minister to tell the committee tonight what has been done in pursuance of that recommendation from the council on manpower. I believe that the house and the country are entitled to know now whether anything has been done in pursuance of that request, and if so, just what has been done.
As the minister knows, plans for such a registration would be extensive. They would take some time to work out, and if conditions become worse time is going to be so very precious. We are not going to have the time to fool around and delay these things again. Action will have to be taken quickly. I would ask the minister to explain just what has been done with regard to those plans for a national registration.
Then, there is another recommendation outlined in this press release, and it deals with the provision of skilled workers for industry and the armed forces. A study of the subject was recommended, and I believe that in the course of the discussion today other members have raised this point. I would ask the minister to tell us definitely what has been done to provide more skilled workers.

Supply-Labour
There was one other recommendation-as a matter of fact there were several other recommendations contained in the press release which I shall not repeat because the minister heard them this afternoon. In the report considerable stress was placed on the use of immigrants coming to Canada. On page 5 of the report we find these words:
Plans have been laid to bring about 150,000 immigrants to Canada during 1951, of whom close to one-half may be workers. Allowances must be made on the other hand for annual emigration which has amounted to between 20,000 and 30,000 during recent years, mostly to the United States.
Will the minister also explain how that plan is progressing; whether we are going to get 150,000 immigrants to Canada during 1951 and whether, as expected, about half of those will be available to help out in industry. Will the minister deal with those questions?

Mr. Chairman, I am sure the
hon. member would not want me to try to give offhand a very good speech

at least I hope it was very good-which I have been looking forward to giving for quite a long time-
You may have to wait a long time.

I hope I shall have the opportunity of giving that speech with respect to the points he mentioned and those mentioned by the hon. member who took his seat just a minute or so ago. Perhaps he will permit me to answer his question quite briefly. First of all with regard to the general comment today on the delay in calling the second meeting of the council, may I say that I have not at any time since the first meeting asked that the second meeting be delayed. Rather have I suggested, even before my friend the hon. member for Nanaimo jogged my elbow the other day, that I felt it would be a good thing for a meeting to be called as early as possible in view of the work intervening. I want to assure my hon. friend that I thought I made it clear in announcing the creation of the council that it was not in any degree under the orders of the Department of Labour or of the government. Two gentlemen in whom most of us have a great deal of confidence were chosen, because of their special qualifications, to act as joint chairmen.
Who are they?
Mr. Norman A. Robertson, clerk of the privy council, and Mr. Arthur MacNamara, my deputy minister.
Yes; but some minister must accept responsibility.

I am accepting responsibility for the receipt of the recommendations from that

council and the advice coming from that council, carrying out what can be carried out in my department and conveying for the consideration of my colleagues those opinions that demand their attention. As to the recommendations that have been read to me tonight, I should like to deal with them more thoroughly at another time on my estimates. But I can tell my hon. friend that the one on the study of registrations has gone on continually in my department and in association with other departments, referring as necessary to individual members of the council from time to time and I understand that a report on that subject will be made to the next meeting of the council.
As to the training of skilled workers for the armed services and for industry, not only has a study been made but arrangements have already been entered into with my colleague, the Minister of National Defence, and we are already carrying out training under that federal-provincial plan for the armed forces, the expense being borne totally by the federal government.
On the other side of the picture, as to training for defence industries, we have found in the investigation so far, in discussing it not only with the provinces but with the industries concerned, that the situation is such now that it is difficult to get any large number of unskilled or semi-skilled men away from the plants to undergo theoretical training in a school for a protracted period. In 1939, 1940 and 1941, I understand, it was possible to do that because there was a much larger reserve of manpower seeking employment. So what we are exploring now is how, if we can do it, to carry out some refinement of the federal training on the job and of making it possible for the plant to have facilities for the training of foremen or in other words to train instructors who in turn might be able to instruct on the job. That matter is receiving, on the part of Mr. MacNamara particularly and officials of the department, and the national employment service, very careful study.
Incidentally, of course, there is going on continually the usual federal-provincial vocational training, on a fifty-fifty basis.
Before the minister leaves that point, may I ask if that dominion-provincial vocational training is not mainly for boys who have just left school, and not for young men trained from the plants?

In the main, it has been; yes. Of course now, for the armed forces, a larger number of more mature men will be going into it, depending on the trades for which they are being trained.

Our role in the Department of Labour with regard to immigration, as my hon. friend knows, is briefly this. We act in association with, and under the policy set out by, the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, providing our facilities within the department, in the unemployment insurance commission and in the national employment services, to assist in placing immigrants who come in without any specified place to work. Although I know that the reports on immigrants arriving and applying are extremely favourable, I would prefer that a more complete report on that subject be given by my colleague the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, and I know he would be glad to give a statement under my estimates if my hon. friend so wishes.

I should like to ask one further question with regard to national registration. How long would it take to complete a registration if one were started say at the end of May? How far have the plans progressed for such a registration, and how long is it estimated the time would be that would be required to complete a registration?

Mr. Chairman, I hope my hon. friend will not cross-examine me and draw me into a discussion of an extremely complex matter when I am here without my notes or anything, and also before there is an opportunity to refer the matter back to the council. But to answer his question in the light of the best information available, with all the preliminary planning, briefing and organization done beforehand, it is estimated that it would take approximately three months.

May I ask the minister if any consideration, has ever been given to using for this purpose the information which will be collected by the census takers?
I know that the returns they make are quite exhaustive. They have the age, the occupation, the citizenship and all that sort of thing. It would seem to me that it is a duplication of work to have another investigation made when we shall have the census returns in a few months. I should like to know whether any consideration has ever been given to that procedure.

I can say that consideration has been given to it; in response also to another question, I can also state that the use of any existing organization of government, namely the census organization, the unemployment insurance commission which has a vast amount of information with regard to workers or our own department, for this purpose of registration-should it ever be necessary, 30709-174
Supply-Labour
after careful thought and weighing of the needs of any future situation-is something which should not be done without the matter being referred to the House of Commons and a complete and full outline given as to the form it should take, and it would only be after further study by the national council. It would be interesting to hear how they feel about the study that has gone on. I think I have approached the matter with a reasonably open mind. I was not here from 1939 to 1944; but I have had an opportunity, as the study has been going on, to see what was done. Some of the hon. members who were here probably know the degree of effectiveness in the fruits of that work, but without referring to that, the thing that does strike one is this: If we were able to take a census this week and provide ourselves with a great mass of information at a very great cost by taking on a large number of employees of government, unless a constant and continual follow-up were maintained, six months from now, nine months from now it would not be worth very much.
I am not putting that down on the debit side at all, but it is a point that has impressed itself upon me, and the question therefore has come up for consideration: Would it be better to do something now, or to do the planning, the staff work, the preparations and the arrangements so that when the time appeared to be essential it could be done quickly?
The minister said that the registration would take about three months. How long will it take to complete the plans preparatory to doing the registration?
I should say within two months.

That would be five months
altogether?
Yes.

Why would it take three
months to do the registration? As I remember the last registration, volunteers helped in every constituency, and it was completed in a very short time. I may be wrong on that, but if my memory serves me that was the position. Everybody helped and the registration was done within a few days. Why would it take three months to complete the registration in 1951?

Again I do not want to be
drawn into a discussion. When I speak of three months I am taking the estimate which was given to me by those who have given careful study to this problem. The impression I got was that while the actual business of getting names and information on cards

Supply-Labour
does not take very long, the real time is taken in compiling the information and putting it in a readily useful form.

I do not want this first item in the labour estimates to pass without saying a word or two on matters that have pressed in upon my mind and puzzled me. At the outset I refer particularly to what I have regarded as rather a delinquent, or shall I say, a slow turnover from a wartime productive basis to a peacetime productive basis. I cannot help thinking that our productive resources in labour manpower could have speeded up the production of wanted goods to a much greater extent than has been done since the end of the war.
When the war ended we expected that we were going to launch into one of the biggest eras of prosperity that the nation had ever seen. Our needs for consumer goods were immense. Through the expansion of war industries during the war and the expansion of the credit facilities of the country, money was more or less plentiful. The productive capacity of the country was perhaps the largest or the greatest that the country had ever seen, and yet somehow or other we did not come to that place where we were producing all that we could.
For years many wanted goods have been in short supply. We were told that there was a backlog of orders. You could not buy cars without putting your name down on the list and waiting for months. I believe that the situation has been alleviated somewhat, but even today you cannot go on the floor of the sales room and buy a car as once you could. Other articles have been in short supply, refrigerators and things of that nature.
It does seem to me that our productive machinery could have been speeded up much more quickly than it was in order to supply Canadians with wanted goods, and goods which they had money to buy. It appears to me that what concerned those governments and labour was the possibility of coming into a period and having to face what our government would regard as an unemployment problem. Their attitude, I have reason to believe, was something to this effect:	We
must not work too hard. Our productive machinery must not be speeded up too fast, or the first thing we know we shall produce too much and we shall have an unemployment problem on our hands.
On that particular point let me say that I regard that view as absolutely fallacious. Instead of looking at the picture and recognizing that unemployment after all is the fruit of a very highly mechanized and

power age in which the burden of toil can be lifted from the shoulders of the worker, giving him more time for life. Instead of regarding the situation as a benefit that should accrue to our civilization, we look at that benefit as being a problem, a problem to be faced. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, the fallacy of that must be recognized both by government, and particularly by the Department of Labour, and also by labour itself. What must be recognized, I believe, is that in the last analysis it is the production of the country that constitutes the real wealth of the nation. It is not necessarily money. Our government policy should be one where we say to labour, "You produce; produce all you can; do not be afraid of overproduction; if there is a period of overproduction we will call it by another name- we will call it underconsumption. So, get your machinery to work and produce all you can. We, as a government, will pursue a financial policy that will distribute the fruits of your labours."
That should be the attitude of the government. But instead of that, we know it is not the attitude of the government. It seems to me its attitude is: "Work like slaves, in order to produce, so that our financial policy may remain as we think it should remain- sound-and we will interpret the term sound as we wish to interpret it." That seems to be the government's policy.
Only yesterday the hon. member for Lethbridge asked the Prime Minister a pertinent question. His question was as to whether the Prime Minister believed that that which is physically possible should be made financially possible, or words to that effect. What did the Prime Minister of this country say? He rose in his place and evaded the question. He did not answer it at all, but flung it back by saying that he was surprised that a member of the Social Credit group should ask such a question. Why should we not ask a question of that kind, and why should not a straightforward answer have been given?
Under the present financial policy of the government, where do we find labour? We find that labour becomes subject to the government's financial policy. I am sure that if the truth be spoken, and if the whole situation were analysed in its proper perspective, labour as well as the government would be able to determine a financial policy that would accrue to labour and to the rest of the citizens of Canada in such a way that labour could enjoy to the very fullest extent the work of their own hands.
I hold in my hand a pamphlet published by the joint labour unions of Canada. It is

a submission on price controls to the government, and is published by the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, the Canadian Congress of Labour, the Canadian and Catholic Confederation of Labour, and the dominion joint legislative committee of the railway transportation brotherhoods. I have read this with some care and I believe it is a good pamphlet; it contains much that is true and is extremely well thought out. But before one finishes reading it he comes to one or two passages which are very significant and revealing. We find this at page 11: Labour will fight, work and sacrifice to preserve freedom. It will not fight, or work, or sacrifice, to preserve any economic system if that system imperils freedom.
That is quite a statement and, placed in its proper perspective, it should be a true statement. But the fact of the matter is that the present financial policy of the government does the very thing that labour says it will not work and sacrifice to avoid. This indicates to my mind that those who have written the pamphlet, despite the fact that it is well thought out and the arguments are good, show a tremendous lack of one thing. There is no evidence whatsoever that the authors of the pamphlet have any knowledge as to the basic monetary principles upon which the economic system functions. It takes for granted that there is nothing basically wrong-I say basically wrong-with the economic system itself.
According to this pamphlet labour admits that the patient is sick. They admit there is something wrong with the body politic. I am not saying they alone, because I think this is characteristic of many people in many organizations and industries throughout the country, as well as in governments. The authors of the pamphlet admit that the body politic is sick, but they are not able to diagnose the seat of the trouble. They admit that a boil breaks out here or a carbuncle breaks out somewhere else, or a rash begins to appear on the body politic-and of course, Mr. Chairman, I am now speaking figuratively. But it never occurs to them that there is anything wrong with the heart or the bloodstream. So when something pops up to dislocate some branch of the economic system they say, "We are sorry that that boil broke out on the neck. We will prescribe this little bit of salve. If we rub it in we may be able to get rid of the boil."
They are giggling.

Or if a carbuncle breaks out on the top of the head so that the body politic cannot wear its hat properly, they say, "Well now, let us prescribe a different kind of 80709-174}
Supply-Labour
salve." So they rub it in again. Someone might even come up with the bright idea of using a scalpel and cutting out the carbuncle. But never do they reach the seat of the trouble.
They may even try an injection, and the body politic rouses itself and appears to take on new strength, only to find that after the injection has worn off the body politic begins to stagger around again. That is the situation. I say, until labour, until industry and until government recognize that the whole economy of the country

labour, wages, prices and all things-is adjusted to a financial policy that will be basically sound, we shall continue to have these troubles with labour and other groups of people, in industry and government alike.
There is another matter too that I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. I did not intend to criticize the labour laws on the statute books of this country because I think they are fair and just. I think the labour code, perhaps for the time being, is one of the best that exists. As time goes on I trust it will be improved, but I do believe that our labour laws, not only nationally but provincially, should guard the right of the individual worker on every occasion. I am not asking questions to be answered. I am intending rather to be provocative. Does the individual worker have his democratic say with freedom and without impairing his right to all the benefits that accrue to labour by reason of organization? I believe that is a question the government should take to its heart and watch most carefully.
I wonder sometimes how integrally related our labour unions are to the labour movements in the United States. I have no objection particularly to a union which because of its particular character may have an international complex. I realize that there are benefits for labour, and perhaps for industry also because industry in some respects has a certain international character. But I believe that we have reason to guard the rights of our individual labour organizations so that they may be free to ply their course and make independent decisions without any interference or coercion from other countries.
I do not want to see happen in Canada what is happening in the United States. The large labour organizations in the United States are fast becoming what I would term a labour monopoly. There was a time when the lords and barons, the princes and kings were looked upon as terrible ogres who were enslaving the worker, and with some degree of accuracy and reason. But that day seems to be

Supply-Labour
slipping from us. The day is arriving, at least in the United States, when the powerful labour leaders have become the barons, lords and kings of the earth.
Monopoly in labour is just as dangerous as monopoly anywhere else. I rather agree with what the hon. member for Kootenay West said a few days ago when he analysed for us the principle of monopoly and stated that sometimes monopoly may be all right if it serves the national or community interest, but that it becomes a danger when it serves a certain section only, regardless of national interest. I trust the government is watching this most carefully because I believe that in the end a monopolistic labour will destroy the rights and freedom of the individual worker.
I am going to leave those thoughts with the minister. I have not asked him any specific questions but I would like him to comment on the first part of my remarks respecting the change-over from wartime production to peacetime production. I know we are gradually slipping back into wartime production, but I do believe that the solution to many of our problems is to place the proper emphasis where it should be placed, to produce all we can and then have the government say, We will settle our financial policy even though we have to change it in order that Canadians may live and enjoy the fruits of their labours.

Mr. Chairman, I intend to be quite brief but I should like to make a few comments on this first item, particularly with respect to the national advisory council on manpower. Before doing that I should like to extend my congratulations to the minister upon assuming this portfolio. I know there were many veterans in Canada who were sorry to see him leave the Department of Veterans Affairs. I am sure that if the minister satisfies labour as he satisfied the veterans of. this country when he was Minister of Veterans Affairs he will be a most successful Minister of Labour.
Before proceeding to what I wish to say tonight I must take issue with the hon. member for Macleod who, as I understood, rather criticized the international aspect of our labour unions. I would draw to his attention that Chrysler is international, that Ford is international, that many other organizations are international. I am quite sure that if there is danger to the national interest or to democratic principles in which we all believe and which we all intend to support and defend, it will come from international capitalism rather than from any other source.

I said that.
[Mr Hansell.]

I am rather intrigued with
this national advisory council on manpower. I believe in principle it is a correct approach to the situation which it has been appointed to advise upon. But many hon. members are not quite sure whether this is a purely paper organization or whether it is really intended to function in the national interest and do the job hon. members expect of it. It has great possibilities and great opportunities if it is given the opportunity to function.
This afternoon the hon. member for Cape Breton South mentioned the capable labour leaders we have on the advisory council, men with talent and ability, and the capable civil servants. He also indicated, however, that these men will not be able to serve satisfactorily on the council unless they are given the opportunity to function as this house expects them to, and unless they have the co-operation of advisory or industrial councils all across Canada, the co-operation of those who are in close touch with local conditions and circumstances. This council can very well deal with over-all policy and general programs, but if its decisions are going to be sound, if they are going to be effective, they must be based on advice and information received from people who are in close touch with local industrial, plant and development conditions.
Therefore I heartily support the suggestion that the government must find the means of having this committee extend its influence throughout the country by co-operation and association with some form of local industrial council which includes representatives of government, labour and management. If the situation is as serious in all constituencies in Canada and presents as serious problems as it does in the constituency I have the honour to represent and in the surrounding country, the council faces a very stiff problem indeed. To illustrate the development projects proposed for the coming year and the next year in the riding I represent, and to some extent in the riding represented by the hon. member for Kootenay East, I would bring to the attention of the committee that the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company has just issued a program of development that calls for the expenditure of $30 million on a new hydroelectric plant, $12 million on the modernization of the Trail lead smelter, $9 million on the development of a phosphate fertilizer plant at Kimberley, $3,200,000 on the development of the zinc plant at Trail, $2,850,000 on the development of the Kootenay river to Kimberley power transmission line, $3 million on the development of the Bluebell

mine, $2,750,000 on the development of the Hudson Bay mine production and preparation.
In addition to the $62,800,000 program proposed by the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, we have a large expansion of mining development. Millions will be put into mining development this year and the year following in Kootenay West alone. Then we have a tremendous expansion of the lumber industry. Nearly all operators in the whole district are expanding their mill operations and their woods operations. At the present time surveys are being made and plans are being drafted for the building of a $20 million pulp mill in the upper Arrow lakes area of my constituency.
Unparalleled prosperity.

In addition, there is a
general private building program in the area involving millions of dollars. In addition, there is the expansion of the telephone service which will involve millions of dollars. There is the extension of the power and light service transmission lines and so on throughout the country in addition to those I have mentioned totalling millions of dollars. In addition, there is the program of the provincial public works department for my area alone totalling something over $6 million, and on top of that there is a federal public works program, including defence production and public works, wharves and so on, totalling close to $1,500,000.
I have drawn to the attention of the committee the enormous development proposed for the constituency I represent and the surrounding country. That development is found pretty well on the same scale throughout the whole of British Columbia. In view of our defence production needs and the tremendous programs that I have mentioned, it is going to take very careful planning and careful assessment of given situations if the two are going to proceed smoothly at the same time. In the building of power dams, in lumber operations and in the development of mining and these large construction projects, large numbers of skilled workmen will be required, men with skills in the particular work being undertaken. In addition a large number of unskilled workers will be required.
Then there is the shifting from one operation to another. You cannot build a huge power plant by suddenly dropping 2,000 men on the job and proceeding with the work. A certain type of people is required for the foundations and the drilling. A certain type is wanted for the concrete work, and then another group for the steel work. The same thing is true with respect to the expansion
Supply-Labour
of the Consolidated plants and the other developments which are going on in my constituency. If we are going to avoid undue travelling about of men while this tremendous development is taking place we shall have to take steps to that end. Men will hear about these things taking place, and not knowing the skills required or the particular type of labour at a particular time they will waste their time and energy travelling to that part of the country seeking work. In some cases when they get there they will find that they are not the type of labourer required at that particular time.
These things pose a tremendous problem. I am quite sure that the national advisory council on manpower, with the best intentions, cannot function efficiently if it is simply going to meet periodically to accept statements of civil servants, figures that have been prepared by the research department, and so on. I believe the council must have in its hands the recommendations of industrial councils or committees composed of representatives of government, labour and management in the areas concerned who are particularly acquainted with the problems involved. Mining problems differ from district to district, from one part of the country to another. Lumbering operations in my constituency are quite different from those carried on at the coast. The building of power plants is a different proposition in the swift waters of the rivers of British Columbia from what it is in the slower flowing waters of eastern Canada. In my opinion the council will have to have the very close co-operation of local committees if it is going to function satisfactorily.
If the minister will see to it that the council has the co-operation of groups all across Canada acquainted with local conditions he will have done something to strengthen the very fibre of democracy because democracy is based upon local and individual responsibility and co-operation no matter whether the development is a provincial or a national program. Before the minister's estimates are concluded, I should like him to explain if he has any plans for such expansion of the services so far as co-ordination and cooperation with the national advisory council on manpower is concerned.

Mr. Chairman, I shall only take a moment on this point. The hon. member for Kootenay West has outlined very clearly in his speech what is intended and what is being carried out in these plans. He outlined the great development in his own constituency. I did not hear from him any observation which would indicate that as

Supply-Labour
yet there is any serious clashing in the sense of providing manpower, but he expressed concern as to the future.
That is right.

I think I am correct in saying that the reason that disruption has not yet occurred has to a great extent been due to the good offices of advisory committees on employment in his area. They have representatives of labour and management serving on these committees, and they are doing an excellent service in advising our regional and local offices of the national employment service. They are very active. When workers are wanted they do not need to go on a wild goose chase, but can find out through these offices where the employment is without spending their money going to various places.
Now, multiply the area in that constituency by all the areas in Canada, Mr. Chairman, and you will see the strength of contact that this national body has available. That was what I meant when I stated in my first announcement in the house that these local employment advisory committees would act in close co-operation with this national body.
There is one other point as to the functions of the council. There seemed to be a suggestion this afternoon that the council was an administrative body in itself, but it is advisory, as the name indicates.

I have to speak on this item, because I do not see any other item in the estimates dealing with this subject. I am glad to know there is going to be such a shortage of manpower in British Columbia. It does not show in the statistics that were published in March, because there was an increase in unemployment there over the previous month. Throughout Canada the same conditions seem to apply, and there were 293,000 listed as unemployed on January 20.
I am not going to speak for the rest of Canada; I am going to speak for Newfoundland and I intend to mention the subject discussed by my friend the member for St. John's East earlier this evening. There is the question of the employment of Newfoundlanders in the iron ore mines on the border of Quebec and Labrador. The question of manpower for the Labrador iron ore mines has been the subject of discussion and legislation in Newfoundland since 1938. Newfoundlanders have been looking forward all these years to getting employment there. Actually there is a mystery, to me at any rate, because no one seems to know anything

about it down in Newfoundland. It is only occasionally that we meet a person who is employed there.
At the present time, I understand, the companies are building a railroad some three hundred miles from Seven Islands into the place where the mine will be operated. As my friend has pointed out, there has been some dissatisfaction amongst Newfoundlanders who have been employed there. In the employment registry office at St. John's on January 25 there were 5,160 registered as unemployed. That was the highest number for any city in Canada east of Quebec. It does not, by any means, represent the number of people who are unemployed, because many people do not think it is worth while to go to the office and put down their names. They have done that and they have never heard anything more about it. They have no faith in it. In addition to that, there are a lot of people like fishermen who are employed seasonally. They do not go to register at all. This is a special year. Because of the low prices which fishermen received for their fish last year, they do not intend to go fishing. There are going to be a great number looking for work. I imagine they had counted on getting some employment in Labrador, either on the railway or in the mine. I should like to know if the minister or his officials have given any consideration to the question of recruiting men to go to these places, or do the men have to find out for themselves how they are going to get employment there?
I know the government has nothing to do with the employment of men there, but I presume that in such an out of the way place the employment commission might be consulted by the companies who are seeking men. I imagine the type of men they want are probably woodsmen and riggers, men who have been working on railway gangs and that type of construction work. I think you could find a great many of them in Newfoundland. When I was at home a great many people came to see me, and a great many people have been writing to me to ask how they can get work in Labrador. I can only refer them to the employment commission in St. John's. My experience has been that it is a sort of accounting office receiving money from those who are employed, and paying out unemployment insurance to those who are not. It is not doing much in regard to obtaining employment for people looking for it. I know that it is nearly eleven o'clock, but perhaps the minister will have a moment to reply.

I shall be happy to give the
hon. member a complete reply under an item in my estimates later, because there are a few aspects of this subject in which I am interested. It applies to my own province as well as his. I shall be glad to outline to him what the feeling of the commission is with regard to the grouping of fishermen under the terms of the act. He will understand at once that there are great difficulties to overcome, but in so far as it is possible to do so we will attempt to carry out the suggestions.
Do I understand the minister to say there is an item under which he can reply to my question?
I shall do so under the unemployment insurance item.

speechtext:
On Wednesday last the Prime Minister announced that the resolution in the name of the Secretary of State for External Affairs would have priority. That resolution concerns the reference of his estimates to the committee on external affairs.
At three o'clock the Prime Minister announced that, if there were an understanding with all parties of the house that we could get through quickly this address concerning the amendment to the British North America Act on old age pensions, he would undertake to move it. I understand that it would not impair the discussion of external affairs which was announced some days ago. I really hope we can succeed in having this put through the house a little more quickly than the first item of the Department of Labour.
Can the minister say what other days next week are also filled?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

On Tuesday we shall move to go into supply, undertaking not to call any new departments, and proceed with
the estimates of national defence.
And Wednesday also?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: And Wednesday also; but please do not ask me about any other days.
I understand then that on Monday external affairs is going on as scheduled?

subtopic: CORRESPONDENCE BETWEEN THE MINISTER OF JUSTICE AND PREMIERS OF THE PROVINCES WITH RESPECT TO OLD AGE PENSIONS CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT

speechtext: Note: We were not supplied by the Hon. Mr. Duplessis with an authorized translation of his letters of March 11, 1951, and April 18, 1951. We desire to emphasize that the unofficial translations which have been prepared here have not been authorized by the Hon. Mr. Duplessis and to that extent are not binding on him.

Office of the Premier
Edmonton, March 6, 1951
The Honourable Stuart S. Garson, K.C.,
Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada,
Ottawa, Canada.
Dear Mr. Garson:
I am in receipt of your letter of the 28th ultimo enclosing copies of the submissions made by the premiers of the various provinces in relation to the proposed amendments to the British North America Act.
I am in agreement with your first suggestion that a new section 95a be enacted reading as follows:
"95a. In each province the legislature may make laws in relation to old age pensions within the province; and it is hereby declared that the parliament of Canada may from time to time make laws in relation to old age pensions in Canada, but no law made by the parliament of Canada in relation to old age pensions shall affect the operation of any law in relation to old age pensions made by a provincial legislature."
While there is no doubt that at the present time the legislature of each province has the power to make laws in relation to old age pensions, nevertheless I can see no objection to repeating the power in section 95a even though redundant, in order that no argument can be raised that it was intended to take this power away.
I have no further suggested amendments to head 2 of section 92.
Yours very truly
(Sgd.) Ernest Manning Premier

Office of the Prime Minister and President of the Council
Toronto, Ontario, March 7, 1951
The Honourable Stuart Garson, K.C.,
Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Mr. Garson:
Your letter of February 28th received.
For reasons which you have very clearly stated, and with which we are in complete agreement, you propose a new section 95A to be in either of the following forms,-
"In each province the legislature may make laws in relation to old age pensions within the province; and it is hereby declared that the parliament of Canada may from time to time make laws in relation to old age pensions in Canada, but no law made by the parliament of Canada in relation to old age pensions shall affect the operation of any law in relation to old age pensions made by a provincial legislature."
or
"It is hereby declared that the parliament of Canada may from time to time make laws in relation to old age pensions in Canada, but no law made by the parliament of Canada in relation to old age pensions shall affect the operation of any law in relation to old age pensions within any province made by the provincial legislature of such province."
Either one of these forms is satisfactory to us. If, therefore, the government of Canada or any of the provinces have a preference for one of these forms it will be quite satisfactory to us.
We trust that the amendment will be effected as soon as possible and the legislation proceeded with as agreed upon.
Sincerely yours,
(Sgd.) Leslie M. Frost
PROVINCE OF BRITISH COLUMBIA Office of the Premier
Victoria, March 8, 1951 Honourable Stuart Garson, LL.D.,
Minister of Justice and Attorney General, Parliament Buildings,
Ottawa, Canada.
My dear Mr. Garson:
I have for acknowledgment your letter of February 28, together with enclosures relating to the proposed constitutional amendments dealing with old age pensions and the indirect sales tax.
I have had our attorney-general and his officials examine your correspondence thoroughly and we have come to the view that the draft in respect of old age pensions to be found on page 3 of your communication satisfactorily deals with this question. It is felt that it grants the necessary power to the parliament of Canada to make laws in relation to old age pensions while at the same time fully preserving provincial rights in dealing with the same question.
In relation to the sales tax amendment, we are satisfied that the amendment suggested by you is quite sufficient for all practical purposes. This amendment, as I gather from your correspondence, is as follows:

Appendix
"2. The raising of revenue for provincial purposes by:
(a)	direct taxation within the province, and
(b)	indirect taxation within the province in respect of the sale of goods (except goods sold for shipment outside the province) to a buyer for purposes of consumption or use and not for resale, at a rate not exceeding three per centum of the sale price, but not so as to discriminate between sales of goods grown, produced or manufactured within the province and sales of goods grown, produced or manufactured outside the province."
With kindest personal regards,
Yours faithfully,
(Sgd.) Byron I. Johnson
Premier
ST JOHN'S, NEWFOUNDLAND Office of the Premier
March 9, 1951
The Honourable Stuart S. Garson, K.C.,
Minister of Justice and Attorney General,
Ottawa, Canada.
Dear Mr. Garson:
Thank you for your letter of the 28th ult. with reference to constitutional amendments in which you enclose copies of correspondence from the various provincial premiers.
I have discussed this matter with the attorney general and it has come before cabinet. As far as Newfoundland is concerned we are prepared to accept what you refer to as your third draft (on page three of your letter), reading-
"It is hereby declared that the parliament of Canada may from time to time make laws in relation to old age pensions in Canada, but no law made by the parliament of Canada in relation to old age pensions shall affect the operation of any law in relation to old age pensions within any province made by the provincial legislature of such province."
but if the other provinces prefer it we would agree to your new draft section 95A (page two of your letter) reading as follows-
"In each province the legislature may make laws in relation to old age pensions within the province; and it is hereby declared that the parliament of Canada may from time to time make laws in relation to old age pensions in Canada, but no law made by the parliament of Canada in relation to old age pensions shall affect the operation of any law in relation to old age pensions made by a provincial legislature."
With respect to the proposed amendment of section 92 (2) it seems to me that the point made by Premier Macdonald may be well taken, and that the amendment with reference to indirect taxation might well be included in section 92 as a new enumerated head (2)	(a). Newfoundland,
however, will accept the ruling of yourself and your advisers in this matter.
Yours faithfully,
(Sgd.) J. R. Smallwood Premier
